text:
@rickysargulesh1053  Yes, and no.
You will get more FPS but for a lot of scenarios even the 7950X will be the bottleneck. 
Igor (from Igorslab) said it perfectly:
"Come on AMD, release the 7000X3D models!"

HOWEVER XD
The same way we kind of reached  a point in mobile phones where new models just don't offer any improvements when it comes to using a messenger (SIGNAL!), browsing the web and taking snapshots the same seems to be true for PC Gaming.
We sit rather closely to the screen so anything beyond 27'' is kind of a stretch. I recently switched to 32'' and tbh it's just more screen out of focus.
I am not sure if it was worth it...
Then 4K at 32''/27'' really is a high enough resolution, especially if we consider that games usually aren't very static.
And now...3080s/6800XTs and everything faster than that are powerful enough to really enjoy playing games at that resolution, especially considering DLSS/FSR.
Now this Google AI found a more efficient way to multiplay matrices which could mean another performance boost on the software side in the future...
The 4090 reached 100 Teraflop.
In 2005 that would have been the fastest computer in the world. It would have been in the top 500 list until 2014.

Combine that with the fact that many modern games include micro transactions and lost the magic of PC gaming that was about "What could we do that would be super awecome?" (Diablo 2 LoD, Jedi Knight 2: Jedi Outcast)

The only thing that calls for that much computing power is VR.
Long story short: I NEED THAT 4090 XDDDDD

text:
Well, looks like they may have a winner in the 40 series after all.
As someone who bought a 3090 at near the top of the market, I'm not all that disappointed. I buy once every 4 years or so, and had already gotten 5 out of my 1080, and that was 5 years of almost-but-not-quite being able to play games at 4k. I've played more games in the last 8 months on my 3090 than the last few years combined simply because it hasn't been a hastle or annoyance.
And then there is the mining aspect. Yes, prices are waaaay down right now. But even still, the 3090 had mined $550 worth of coin before the eth merge. I'm expecting a 6x bump in btc price after the next halving cycle, but even if it is "only" 4x, that becomes a free GPU. Time will tell if that pans out the way I am expecting, but a free card that is overpriced is still cheaper than a cheaper card when there is nothing it can do to pay for itself. But... You know... These are the lies we tell ourselves to sleep better at night lol.

At any rate, the other GPUs we purchased were at a steal leading up to the merge. So my kids got a 3070ti and 3080 for dirt cheap. And as they only have 1080p 60hz displays that is going to be plenty for a very long time, so no worries there.

I think the biggest question with the 40 series, is what the demand will be. These are the first Gen cards that can really do ray tracing which is cool. But not a lot of titles yet that make it the feature that it eventually will be. And for non rt games, even a 3080 can keep up well in 4k. Unless we see a flood of ray trace games, or 8k displays... I'm not sure what the upgrade value is for gamers on the 30 series. We have finally hit that level of "good enough" performance like we did on the cpu side with the 2000 series sandy bridge. Sure later CPUs were still faster, but no workload justified an upgrade for 8 years! Without a higher workload, I am curious what the road map looks like on the GPU side going forward.

text:
Something to keep in mind, that I feel is one of the most important considerations, that only comes up every handful of years. 

We are between generations still largely. And right on the heels of UE5 games being delivered. This means that we should expect a fairly hefty jump in "max card performance" requirements in the coming year as we get more UE5 and other "modern" engine games released. In general, we are just now starting to see more games drop off of XBO and PS4 support. Meaning the baseline target being the PS5 and XBS with raytracing. 

So in some ways, the 4090 could be the best option if you currently play at 2k/4k. Especially so if you have a display that supports 2k@240/4k@120. 

Even with this though, I wouldn't scramble to grab a 4090 unless you know a game is out/about to release that is going to require a 4090 to hit those 80+ at 4k, or 200+ @2k.

text:
It looks like the two Sense pins on the 12VHPWR connector aren't being used (yet) for any clever serial protocol.

Instead, either one or both pins are grounded by the cable (or plug), to let the card know the maximum current it can draw from the PSU.

If both Sense pins are left open (pulled high by resistors), the card will only draw a max of 100W at start-up, and 150W boost.

If both Sense pins are pulled to Ground (likely just by the joined ground pins on the PSU side of the adapter), the card can draw a max of 375W at start-up, then 600W boost.

(so I guess that's 31.25 Amps then 50 Amps max.)

I don't get how that would work for the detection of three plugs from the PSU to the adapter, though. lol

Unless they have a diode or something in the adapter itself?
author: @electronash

text:
Oh, the four extra pins are labelled CARD_PWR_STABLE, CARD_CBL_PRES#, Sense 0, and Sense 1.

CARD_PWR_STABLE is just a "power good" signal which goes from the card back to the PSU. That's an optional thing that the card can use to tell the PSU if the card has a fault of some kind.

CARD_CBL_PRES# has the # at the end, which denotes an Active-Low signal. The card can use that to tell the PSU that the cable is connected fully, or something.

(a bit like on most modern GPUs, they use one of the "ground" pins on the PCIe power connector to detect the cable is plugged in.)

Still doesn't explain how the three-plug adapter for the 4090 works. lol

It would work out if only two of the PSU plugs were needed to tell the card it can draw the max 600W (boost), but I don't see how it would know the third plug is connected?

text:
1% and 0.1% lows specifically measure driver workload on the CPU, and has nothing to do with the GPU hardware itself, because stutter is mostly caused by shader compiles and resource creation (all CPU-side operations). The rest is caused by other CPU-side operations.

Also these numbers can completely vary depending on whether the shader cache is populated or not, and that cache can get eliminated upon new driver installs or running another game (where a shader cache exceeds the caching limits and gets rid of the shaders).

text:
The recent Ethereum(and possibly COVID) fueled boom and bust for video cards has put NVidia in an interesting position:
 - They had to ramp up production of 30-series cards and now have overstock
 - They just had several record years for sales and profit margin and now things are getting a lot more competitive and, maybe, 'back to normal'.
 - They just developed a new architecture which is way ahead of their competition and their previous generation.
So what do they do moving forward?
 - Delay or seriously nerf the lower-ranked cards in this series so they sell more of their 30-series in the mean time...knowing they are giving room to their competitors?
 - Release the lower 40-series cards soon...but at significantly higher costs than their 30-series counterparts...still giving competitors room with regard to value?
 - Release the lower 40-series cards at a reasonable cost so they will compete more strongly?
One would have to guess they will do what they feel will make them the most money

text:
OC power consumption of 666 watts.
The perfect card to play  DOOM on.

The 4080 16 GB has 59.375% of the shading units that a 4090 has and the 4080 12GB has a mere 46.875%.

Extrapolating those figures onto TechPowerUp's relative performance 4K resolution graph, that puts the 4080 16GB a bit below the 3080 Ti and the 4080 12GB a bit above the 3070 Ti.  

That's disconcerting given the actual 4080 12GB will almost certainly not scale as well due to the large difference in memory bus between the 4080 12GB and the 4090.  So in fact we might see a 4080 12GB that performs on par with a 3070 (or potentially worse assuming the dip to a 192-bit memory bus only drops performance a few percentage points).

I'm not sure I see a universe where the 4080 12GB makes any sense anywhere near $900 USD.  Even if you assume that the 4090 is being held back somewhat at 4K by current CPUs, it's not being held back to the extent where the extremely cut down 4080 12GB is going to find 50% extra performance to justify it's insane price tag.

To me this just seems like Nvidia is pushing the only cards really improving performance per dollar further up the stack to increase margins.  It's crazy to think that GPU prices that were once considered insane are now being rationalized by some because Nvidia continues to find innovative ways to structure it's SKUs to extract maximum profits from customers.

Also, TPU discovered that the 4090 has a higher than normal driver overhead.  It would be interesting to see if the 4000 series in general will all require a powerful CPU.

text: Go watch Linus's video about 8k or the old GN videos about 8k, it's not that the card couldn't play some games at 8k this time around; it IS that 8k is functionally useless as a resolution for gaming. The framerates are low and the optimal viewing distance is far enough away that you can't see the increase in pixels. Basically 4k is enough pixels for standard aspect ratio monitors and TVs. Where 8k makes a difference is ultra widescreen curved, (where you aren't trying to look at the whole screen at once) and virtual reality (where you also can't see the whole screen at once).

EDIT 2: Never mind, LTT just published that they inadvertently had FidelityFX on, invalidating their results. Their new numbers are even worse than here. So, meh!

EDIT: How are the raytracing numbers so vastly different between this test and what Anthony at LTT showed?! And even if massive difference in Cyberpunk can be explained by assuming that different portions of the game were tested, the raytracing performance uplift compared to previous gen (not just in Cyberpunk!) was also much, much higher there! I'm puzzled.

Original comment: To me, after the impressions have settled a little bit, the main takeaway is that the 4090 is still meh for raytracing, while being overkill for everything else, which makes it kind of pointless. 

The target resolution for a card that is this big, weighs this much, draws this much power and costs $1600 is 4k and at that res, with raytracing, the GPU manages 70-80fps in today's and yesterday's titles (Control is a game from 2019!) and in Cyberpunk (itself a 2020 title) it needs DLSS to achieve even that; if we expect that the games coming out from this moment forward will have more advanced and thus more demanding RT implementations than those from 2019-2020, then the performance is underwhelming for a top of the line third generation raytracing capable GPU. And, as I said, if we put raytracing aside, well, then this card is an absolute overkill, from absolutely every angle.

author: @jermasus

text: @jermasus  I know you were joking,  but that WAS the case with some AIBs. The 3090 has VRAM on the back of the board, as well as the front. Every manufacturer thought they could get away with the same bottom of the barrel thermal pads that they used with GDDR6, but 6x gets way hotter. Some AIBs straight up didn't put thermal pads on the VRAM on the back of the board. I did a thermal pad swap on my Zotac 3080 AMP Holo (the only card I could get "retail" during the pandemic), and my VRAM temps went from 106C down to 72C. There is absolutely no reason they should've cheaped out that much on a card that costed $1,000 directly from the manufacturer.

text:
I'm presently surprised. When NVidia claimed 2x performance compared to 3090 ti, I thought they were absolutely full of shit and that 1 scenario in 1 game got a 2x number for them to claim and that the real average uplift was going to be maybe 20% without including any upscaling technology like DLSS. But, to actually see roughly 60% uplift isn't bad. I still wish NVidia didn't pull this shit with the exaggerated 2x claim, and it really would be nice if the high end wasn't climbing into the territory of not even wanting these cards installed during non-gaming use. I know these cards really don't use much if you're not gaming, but it still wouldn't make me comfortable having a card that can pull 450w all on its own. I don't even use my desktop with a 3090 in it very much because my laptop as a whole uses less energy than just my 3090.

But, it seems that the unfortunate truth is that the high end cards will be concerned with pulling as much power as they can without failing in the name of an extra few FPS. Simply becoming more efficient isn't enough. I hope those who buy 4090s enjoy their ridiculous energy bills.

text:
The 4080 16 GB has 59.375% of the shading units that a 4090 has and the 4080 12GB has a mere 46.875%.

Extrapolating those figures onto TechPowerUp's relative performance 4K resolution graph, that puts the 4080 16GB a bit below the 3080 Ti and the 4080 12GB a bit above the 3070 Ti.  

That's disconcerting given the actual 4080 12GB will almost certainly not scale as well due to the large difference in memory bus between the 4080 12GB and the 4090.  So in fact we might see a 4080 12GB that performs on par with a 3070 (or potentially worse assuming the dip to a 192-bit memory bus only drops performance a few percentage points).

I'm not sure I see a universe where the 4080 12GB makes any sense anywhere near $900 USD.  Even if you assume that the 4090 is being held back somewhat at 4K by current CPUs, it's not being held back to the extent where the extremely cut down 4080 12GB is going to find 50% extra performance to justify it's insane price tag.

text: Well basically the splitter connector is still a „dumb“ connector which just wires the „ground“ or 0V rail to one of the 4 sense pins on the new connector. The intelligence is in the card not the connector, meaning you could hardwire all 4 sense pins to 0V and only use 1 cable in case you wanna start a fire

text:
Thank you for mentioning the jump over the 3090, because a generational uplift is over the SAME product in a stack.  To me it's looking like 75 - 100% in general which is mind blowing for a single gen, but what was predicted with Nvidia moving off a slower node to the best node in the world, TSMC N4.  And this also drives cost.  I know this comment will get the hate, but this is a much better deal than last gen 3090 Ti where for most the time it was selling around this price range or even higher.

To me this is the first REAL 4K gaming GPU, where you don't have to turn a lot of settings down and it can pump out the fps.  I'm waiting for the following generation though because I want that performance at lower power consumption which is what will happen with the 5000 series and RDNA 4.


So point of contention with your commentary about buying advice.  This is a HELL of a 4K gaming GPU which is the only reason why people should be buying it anyway, since the 6900 XT and 3090 and 3090 Ti are already premiere 2K gaming GPUs.  This is something that gets paired with that big shiny 4K OLED TV with a PC input made for gaming and enjoy the splendor of what modern hardware can give in gaming.  In which case you DO want RT most the time.


Also, if I'm buying this I'm not pairing it with anything except Zen 4 Vcache, where I think some of those CPU limitations will disappear.

text:
It seems like gaming at 4K with RT enabled has finally reached a performance level that’s compelling enough to consider.  Without RT enabled, it seems like you should probably be running everything with super sampling enabled to make use of all that extra performance—which might even look better than it would with RT.  Lighting effects are cool, but crisp clear images at extreme distances are far more useful than RT, especially since the look of cube mapping with parallax looks almost as good and tends to be more than good enough while you’re playing.

That said, if I had one of these, I’d probably just load up the RTX version of Minecraft because it’ll finally run well.

text: Switching power supplies have a loop response time relative to their switching frequency. Secondary to that is the bulk capacitance which acts as reserviors for these minute (but substantial) spikes.  The GPU's regulation must have adequate input capacitance to smooth those spikes as the loop back to the supply and its time centric response is "at a distance" as well. So that factors in to surge recovery. This is really interesting as GPU core (CUDA in this case) activities tend to be variant for games.  But when you add tensor cores and ray tracing the spikes will likely get bursty and more frequent depending on the game or non-game application. It will be really interesting to see the spikiness with AI benchmarks, FoldingAtHome etc. Each application has its own "power signature".  Kudos to NVIDIA (and TSMC of course) - quite an achievement.

text:
ROFL @WCCFTech labeling frametime as "latency" for the DLSS3 vs DLSS2 comparison.
Example of how this is ridiculous: No way a DLSS3 80fps (40fps rendered + 40fps AI generated) will feel smoother than 60fps rendered. Even though its frametime is better, it's the rendered frames that count, because AI generated frames don't take user input (keyboard + mouse) into consideration when generating frames, so when talking about latency and input lag it's actually 40fps vs 60fps, not 80fps vs 60fps.
Anyone can create a script that copy/paste each rendered frame 2 times before the next rendered frame is displayed and claim that their game is running @60fps from 20fps and "latency" (frametime) is 2x better, even though the game's response time in both instances will feel absolutely the same, regardless of how many "false" frames you insert inbetween rendered frames.
It's just like old school Vsync. 60fps Vsync off will have way less input lag than 60fps Vsync on, even though both frametimes are the same (1s/60fps = 16,7ms per frame).

text: 12:30 Well, if people are stupid and try to pair a $1700 card with a cheap $100 power supply they deserve the results they get. I've used nothing but 1200W+ PSU's for the past 20 years, with the goal being to never let it exceed 50% full load rating (it will last far longer than pushing at 90-100% 24/7, some from 15 years ago still work fine). My current Ryzen 7950/3080/64GB ram/23 HDD's (digital packrat PC) runs on a 1550W Thermaltake titanium ($500 at the time I bought it), maybe 70% load even when all 23 drives are spinning at once (rare, usually during annual Backblaze backup refreshes). Easy fix to handle transient spikes without buying a new 12v v3 PSU is put a quality low-leakage low-esr 5 Farad or so car audio capacitor across the 12v into the card if necessary. That removes the same transients that the audio amp causes when the bass punches and causes a 10x-normal power demand spike a few times a second.

text: Can you guys start benchmarking ultra-wide resolutions as well? I know they are still not the norm for the gaming market, but I have to imagine the target audience is about the same size as 4k gaming. I wasted a lot of time trying to diagnose what was "wrong" with my computer because I was never hitting anywhere close to other published 1440p framerates for games I played. I knew that being an ultra-wide would affect it a little, but I didn't do the actual math until today to understand how significant it actually is. A 3440 x 1440 (WQHD 1440p monitor) has almost 35% more pixels than its standard width brother (2560 x 1440), and that ends up having a huge impact on the framerates in game. Some more numbers for comparison's sake, 4k has 125% more pixels than QHD (2560 x 1440) and is only 67% more pixels than WQHD (3440 x 1440).

text:
Awesome review :)

Just one nit to pick: While MOSFETs do have TjMax between 130 and 180C depending on node size, there is a power derating curve that is applied beyond a specific junction temperature. If you're measuring the package temp, you have to add between 30 and 40C to the reading to arrive at Tj. It is typical to reach half the allowed power dissipation at Tj ~80C. It is also handy to remember that memory, for example is basically a bunch of MOSFET junctions, as is most of the graphics processor.

text:
No, no it DOES NOT know how many cables are attached to the connector when using the squid. At all. Period. It is literally impossible without the gfx card running advanced emf diagnostics on it unless they're wiring in reference points to the signal pins within the squid itself.

Using a squid WILL NOT leave the card with the ability to pick an appropriate power target. It will just suck what juice it can.

The reason it didn't POST at all is because by specification. Floating pins (unconnected) means the card cannot use more than 150W. It probably knows it cannot stay in that power window and doesn't post. The squid undoubtedly has the appropriate pins powered to tell the card, "yea just go ham".

text: Generally saying MOSFETs can take 120C okay is missing the point and a little understanding on why temperature is an issue for electronics in general but power devices specifically. The amount of heat output from the FET (heat dissipation) is derated with temperature which means technically FETs can operate at 120C but with what power dissipation budget (SOA)? This depends on the PSU, the load design and the FET used so a FET will work fine at 120C in one design but only 80C in another design.

text:
As an engineer, I'm very impressed with the FE cooler. They talked a lot about it, but damn didn't they prove it. Excellent balance across the whole PCB. 
The performance uplift is impressive, but the power draw at stock and OC and especially the cable solution (Mechanically and thermally, as someone who needs a 180 degree turn in the GPU cable right after the plug) are a big issue for me. 
I'll stick to my 3080 TUF OC (Lucked out and bought it at nearly MSRP in 2020) and wait for the next generation. By then the power draw should come down and the ATX 3.0 (Maybe even 4.0 to get a stable GPU connector) PSUs should've matured enough to alleviate any spikes and stability issues (My 3080 TUF already had issues with 2 1000W name brand PSUs).

IMO They should ship a 2 slot cover with every card (At least offer an option), so people who will use custom watercooling can use them in vertical brackets and cases smaller than a tower big enough to fit the FE.


Damn, those 3090 Ti got bent over a barrel. But they probably won't care and buy a 4090.

author: @ICEMANZIDANE

text: It has to be higher there's no way it can't be unless NVIDA has figured out magic. Those extra frames aren't coming from the game engine but from the driver and the card. Inputs are only gonna update at the rate of the game engine which is what determines latency. If the game with DLSS 3 is putting out like 120FPS when in reality the game engine is only outputting half of that then you aren't magically gonna get 120FPS like latency it has to at least the latency you'd get at 60FPS. That only get worse the bigger the gulf between the actually rate at which the game engine is updating and how many fake frames are being used. That said there's an argument to be made for weather or not the increase is enough to make a noticeable or big difference to the end user.
